passage: The evening her parents told her they were separating, Lalremsiami walked out of the room and shut her door. For weeks she would not eat dinner if her father, Eshaan, sat at the table; she blamed him for everything. At night she cried into her pillow for the house with two parents and the Sunday breakfasts, but at school she told her friends, "I'm fine, honestly." She kept up her football practice anyway. In her head one quiet question kept going: her fights with her mother, Uma, over marks, the exam she failed. Had she pushed them apart? One night Uma found her awake, and Lalremsiami finally asked. Uma said, "No. This is between your father and me. It is not your fault, and we both love you." Eshaan said the same on the phone the next day. Lalremsiami cried properly then, and told her best friend how much she missed the old family. Under the anger, she realised, she had mostly been sad. Months later, on a Sunday, she visited Eshaan's new flat, ate his lopsided pancakes and saw two flawed people who did better living apart. She still missed the old house. She said so, and Eshaan nodded.

qa.q: What would Lalremsiami not do if her father sat at the table?
qa.a: She would not eat dinner.

qa.q: How did Lalremsiami's feelings toward her father change between the first weeks and the months afterwards?
qa.a: At first she blamed Eshaan and would not sit with him while her grief and her secret question about her fights stayed hidden; after her parents said it was not her fault and time passed, she visited his flat and saw both parents as flawed people who did better living apart.

qa.q: What was Lalremsiami feeling when she told her friends "I'm fine, honestly"?
qa.a: She was hiding sadness and grief, trying to look fine while crying at night.

qa.q: What could Lalremsiami do next to look after herself?
qa.a: She could keep up her football practice, keep talking to a friend or counsellor, keep visiting Eshaan and stay honest with both parents.

grounding: A teenager moves through blame, hidden grief, guilt about her own part and later acceptance as her parents separate.

passage: Three weeks after Saurabh's father died, his classmates were talking about the fest again, and nobody asked how he was. It hurt. In the canteen he told two friends, "I'm not okay. I don't need advice. Just sit with me sometimes." They did. At home his mother handed him the bank papers and the electricity bill as if he were the grown-up. Saurabh felt proud and heavy at once, and told her he would help but wanted his uncles involved so that he was not doing everything alone. At night he asked the ceiling, "How could God let him go?" and felt a little ashamed of his anger. He told an elder relative, who said the questions were allowed and that they could sit with them together. In the library Gurleen, who had lost her friend Sachin last term, showed him a letter in her notebook. She kept replaying the last chat, when she had left his message unanswered. She wrote the letter to Sachin, read it out to Saurabh, and told him about the day they had laughed on the terrace. Saurabh listened, then shared a memory of his father laughing at his own bad jokes.

qa.q: What did Saurabh ask his two friends to do?
qa.a: He asked them to just sit with him sometimes.

qa.q: How did Saurabh's needs with his classmates differ from what his mother needed from him?
qa.a: With classmates who had moved on, he named what he needed and asked them to sit with him; with his mother, who leaned on him as if he were the grown-up, he offered help but brought in his uncles so that he would not carry it alone.

qa.q: What was Gurleen feeling as she kept replaying the last chat with Sachin?
qa.a: She felt guilty and sad, regretting that she had left his message unanswered.

qa.q: What could Gurleen do next to carry her guilt?
qa.a: She could keep sharing memories of Sachin, talk with people she trusts like Saurabh and remind herself that she could not have known.

grounding: Two grieving students show peers' indifference, a parent's leaning, anger at God and guilt over a last message to a friend who died.

passage: Her boss Jagdish leaned on Leela's desk and said the quarterly figures should be "rounded up a bit" and the safety issue held back until after the audit, adding that people who were not flexible found visas hard to renew. Leela's chest went cold. Losing the job, the visa and the reference seemed too large, and for a day going along felt sensible. That evening she wrote down what he had said, the date and the time, and emailed: "To confirm, you've asked me to change the figures and delay the disclosure. I can't do that, but I can prepare accurate numbers." She called the company ethics line and refused to be the only signature. Arnab, a colleague from accounts, caught her by the lift. "Last year I signed one of these," he said. "I've felt sick ever since." With Leela beside him he told the ethics officer, who took notes, said the report would reach the compliance head that day, and explained how Arnab could correct the records. Two weeks later both were moved off the big client, and someone called them troublemakers. Leela kept her emails, asked a lawyer friend which regulator to contact, and leaned on her sister and two friends. She felt afraid, yet whole.

qa.q: What did Leela write down that evening?
qa.a: She wrote down what Jagdish had said, the date and the time.

qa.q: How did Leela's reaction to Jagdish's pressure differ from Arnab's earlier choice, and what did they do together?
qa.a: Arnab had signed one such paper last year and felt sick ever since, while Leela wrote down the instruction, replied politely that she could not do it and refused to be the only signature; together they told the ethics officer and Arnab corrected the records.

qa.q: What was Leela feeling when Jagdish mentioned visas being hard to renew?
qa.a: She felt cold with fear, worried about losing her job, visa and reference.

qa.q: What could Leela do next now that she has been sidelined?
qa.a: She could keep her emails as records, follow up with the right regulator and keep leaning on her sister and friends.

grounding: A worker faces a boss's pressure to fudge figures, fear of losing a visa, a colleague's guilt after going along once, and retaliation after reporting.

passage: On Saturday morning Kashish folded a sheet of paper and drew a yellow kite with a smiling sun for Elizabeth's birthday. Her heart hopped as she handed it over at the party, and her mouth stretched into a big smile. Elizabeth had a pile of shop-bought presents, but she kept holding the kite and said it was the best one. Then Elizabeth gave Kashish a drawing of two girls holding hands under a rainbow. "This is us." Kashish said, "Thanks, it's so pretty!" and hugged the paper to her chest, warm all over. She wanted to give something back, so on Sunday she made a card with a crooked red heart for her Papa, Saurabh, and gave it to him while he chopped tomatoes. He wiped his hands, read the wobbly letters aloud and fixed the card to the fridge with a magnet, right in the middle. "Here, where everyone can see," he said. Kashish stood looking at the fridge for a long time.

qa.q: What did Kashish draw on the card for Elizabeth?
qa.a: Kashish drew a yellow kite with a smiling sun.

qa.q: How did Kashish's giving to Elizabeth differ from her receiving Elizabeth's drawing, and how did it lead to the card for Papa?
qa.a: She gave a kite she made herself with a big smile and Elizabeth loved it; when she received a drawing she hugged it and felt warm and loved, which made her want to give something back, so she made a card for Papa.

qa.q: What was Kashish feeling as she hugged Elizabeth's drawing?
qa.a: She felt loved and warm all over.

qa.q: Why did Saurabh putting the card on the fridge matter to Kashish?
qa.a: He treasured her small gift, so she learned that giving is valued and that her own effort matters.

grounding: A young child gives a homemade card to a friend, receives a friend's drawing with thanks and gives Papa a card he proudly displays.

passage: Sumit's hands shook whenever Ms. Elizabeth called on him. She was strict, and he was sure she liked Ira and Dev better, because she smiled at their answers and never at his. He felt invisible. After class he asked, "Ma'am, can you show me the last sum again?" She sat with him, drew boxes on the board and said, "I'm strict because I want you to try." His hands stopped shaking. Meanwhile his favourite, Ms. Fernandes, scolded him in art for paint spilled on the floor, though Dev had knocked the jar. Sumit was shocked. On Friday he told her politely, "I felt sad when you said it was me. It was Dev's elbow." She paused and said, "I got that wrong. I'm sorry." The next week a substitute teacher, Ms. Desai, held up his drawing before everybody and said, "Is this a potato?" Everyone laughed, and Sumit wished he could vanish. At home he told his father, Kamal, who said a teacher can correct a child without laughing at them. Next morning Kamal went with him to the principal, who thanked them and promised to speak to the substitute that day.

qa.q: What did the substitute teacher ask about Sumit's drawing?
qa.a: The substitute teacher asked whether it was a potato.

qa.q: How did Sumit's way of handling Ms. Elizabeth's strictness differ from the way he handled Ms. Fernandes's mistake?
qa.a: With Ms. Elizabeth he felt afraid and invisible, so he asked her for help after class and saw her softer side; with Ms. Fernandes he was shocked by her unfairness and politely told her how he felt, and she apologised.

qa.q: What was Sumit feeling when the substitute teacher held up his drawing and everyone laughed?
qa.a: He felt humiliated, so much that he wished he could vanish.

qa.q: Why was going to the principal with his father a good step for Sumit?
qa.a: It let the adults raise it with the school, since a teacher should correct a child without shaming them.

grounding: A child meets four kinds of teacher moments: fear of a strict teacher, feeling invisible, a favourite's unfair scolding and a substitute's mockery.

passage: Gurpreet posted a photo of her rangoli and checked the likes every two minutes. Seven. Her mood sank. That night she scrolled through her friend Rajni's beach photos and felt left out, until she remembered they were highlights and sent Rajni a voice note. "Looks amazing, tell me everything!" Rajni called back and talked for an hour about the sunburn and the lost flip-flop. At school her classmate Harish held up his new phone and read out his test marks. Gurpreet sensed he was comparing to feel taller, so she said, "Nice score," then asked about the cricket match instead of racing to top him. Later she noticed the loop: post, wait, feel low. She muted three accounts that made her feel less, and posted a clip of her grandmother's recipe because she wanted to. It spread to thousands of views overnight, and the rush made her giddy. She enjoyed it for a day. When the numbers slipped the next week, she still liked the video, and she called Rajni to say the recipe worked. 😊

qa.q: How many likes did Gurpreet's rangoli photo have?
qa.a: It had seven likes.

qa.q: How did Gurpreet's response to Rajni's holiday photos differ from her response to Harish showing his marks?
qa.a: With Rajni she felt left out, remembered they were highlights and reached out with a voice note; with Harish she sensed he was comparing, stayed warm and did not compete.

qa.q: What was Gurpreet feeling as she checked the likes every two minutes?
qa.a: She felt anxious and low, as if her worth depended on the number.

qa.q: What could Gurpreet do to keep her worth separate from the numbers?
qa.a: She could keep posting for reasons of her own, keep muting accounts that make her feel less and message a friend instead of scrolling. 🙂

grounding: One teenager moves through posting for likes, envy of friends' photos, a friend's flashing and a post that goes viral, and keeps her balance.
